description: We are a passionate team of student innovators based in Valencia City, Bukidnon, gearing up for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Inspired by the traditional Filipino word for star (Tala), our team is on a mission to explore deep-space open data and create beautiful, impactful solutions for "The Next Frontier."
summary:
We developed a website that finds a suitable place on earth that analogs moon and mars for the Artemis Campaign to have a viable choices to simulate. It paves the way to efficiently simulate NASA missions, particularly Artemis Campaign. 
It's important because it provides NASA the information they need and find suitable locations on earth to simulate their missions here on earth before actually implementing it on the Moon/Mars, which can potentially reduce mission cost, Time efficient, safer simulations, faster development.
details:
Terra Sync. is an interactive 3D globe for finding and comparing Earth analogs of Moon and Mars exploration sites. Users can rotate and zoom the globe and fly to guided views of analog sites, such as the McMurdo Dry Valleys (for Shackleton Crater), Hawaii and Iceland (for Marius Hills), Haughton Crater (for Arcadia Planitia), and Lava Beds and the Atacama (for Pavonis Mons). Each site is paired with its lunar or Martian counterpart and broken down by dimension: geology, terrain, temperature, water and ice, and subsurface features like lava tubes. For each pairing it also states where the analogy breaks down, such as gravity, vacuum, radiation, and atmosphere. An adjustable sunlight control lets users compare lighting conditions, which matters for polar sites. The globe is built with Three.js and WebGL and uses static NASA-derived imagery composites, not live observations.
It helps students, educators, and enthusiasts see why particular places on Earth are used to prepare for Moon and Mars missions, and what each place can and cannot teach us. It runs in a modern browser, with controls for both desktop and mobile.
The project aims to make planetary analog research easier to understand and to show that no single Earth site matches another world in every way. Presenting each analogy as strong in some dimensions and weak in others encourages people to look beyond “looks similar” and think about the processes behind it. It is intended for education and discovery, not navigation or precise scientific measurement.
We used JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Three.js for 3D graphics and Vite to build and run the site. Rendering uses WebGL in the browser, and the site includes NASA-derived Earth imagery and a star catalog. Analog comparisons draw on open lunar and Martian data from NASA and other space agencies. No special hardware is needed beyond a computer or phone with a WebGL-capable browser.
Instead of presenting a single “best match” site, it treats analogy as multi-dimensional, scoring each Earth location separately on geology, topography, temperature, ice, and subsurface conditions. Users explore these comparisons spatially on a rotatable globe with guided views, so they can see for themselves where an Earth site is a strong analog and where it falls short.
We considered ease of use, responsive desktop and mobile layouts, and reduced-motion preferences. We also considered the sources and licensing of imagery and data, and we label the visuals as illustrative composites and not live observations. For the analogs themselves, we considered scientific honesty: each pairing explains what the Earth site cannot reproduce, such as reduced gravity, the lunar vacuum, and the thin Martian atmosphere.
